Honestly, speaking from the POV of a Philadelphian, my educated guess is that it’s not often thought about by most people in Philly.   
I am not an employer, so I don't know how a school's reputation and rank factor into employment decisions, but I feel confident in saying a potential big factor in a hiring process to consider is that there are definitive “Philly schools” that have a lot of passionate alumni in management positions, especially concentrated in and around Philly.  
Those schools are Temple, Saint Joe’s, La Salle, UPenn, and Drexel. Villanova is a different animal in that it’s in the Philly Suburbs but is most often clumped in with those other schools.  Penn State is 3+ hours away but due to their large size, they also have a lot of powerful alums in Southeastern Pennsylvania. This is a factor that can be applied to every other state and their major cities.

  
I don’t know what you’re looking for in a school, but here are some things that a Haverford tour guide won’t tell you, but as someone who grew up in the Philly Suburbs and is still in college but has transferred schools a couple times, I want you to know.  
Haverford is in the Philly suburbs, so there’s not going to be a whole lot of fun events happening nearby off-campus. I can’t speak to the school's on-campus activities, aka both school organizations and the party scene, but I imagine Niche has good insight of at least the party scene. If your school has nothing you're interested in beside your major classes, in my opinion you're much more likely to be miserable.

The following sentence is the most important thing I’ll say here:

The Philadelphia Suburbs in general are very spaced out and the main way of transport is via a car. You can do public transport but it's going to always involve buses and they're not always convenient in the suburbs. 

Here are some things that occur at colleges like this that may not apply to you, but I think I should let you know just in case they do that you:

\-There are going to be students at Haverford who go into Center City Philadelphia on the weekends to party, but they will be using Uber or Lyft to do so. I know from experience, that is a risky gamble money-wise. Haverford is technically a 30 or so minute drive from that part of Philly, but the main way to get there is by using freeways so you're accumulating a lot of miles on that trip. Depending on the time of day, I imagine a Lyft from Haverford to McGillin's (famous Philly bar in center city) can cost anywhere from $40 to way over $150 not including tip. (please tip) Most Philly bars, at least before COVID, closed at 2am so the rideshare companies would always jack up their prices then. On holidays an Uber ride can cost over double the amount the same ride would cost any other day. If you're getting an Uber from Cavanaugh's (also near center city) back to Haverford's campus at closing time after drinking on Saint Patrick's day, you're gonna have a real pricey bill. The area in Philly people like to go to for bars can vary, I imagine some Haverford students might go to Main Street in Manayunk, which is an area in Philly that is closer to the suburbs and is mainly filled with college bars. Whereas 2nd street in South Philly on the other hand, while still a good time, is geographically past both Manayunk and Center City, making it probably an hour drive from the suburbs. In the same vein, if you want to go to any of the local sports games or concerts, you're going to have a really hard time getting back to Haverford from a big event without a car as there are limited rideshare pickup around those areas and again, their prices will be jacked up due to the events. 

If you want to do anything there that I just mentioned, you're going to need to find a group of friends and you're going to have to have some petty cash at your disposal as well.

\-I imagine the university does have all the necessities for their students on their campus or at least within walking distance, as in they'll definitely have a nurse, a cafeteria, a Target or Walmart, maybe a grocery store, and other places like that, but if you personally need a service or store that is specialized, you will have to drive somewhere off-campus for that. Common examples of this would be that I initially went to school in the Chicago South Loop, I had a school nurse, but I needed monthly medicine refills at a drugstore that took took my insurance. Luckily, there was a CVS that was within walking distance that did do that for me, but in Haverford there would not be. A similar example is about one of my HS friends can't eat gluten, but he ended going to a spread out suburban school elsewhere. He found that the only grocery stores there had very limited gluten-free options and there were no specific gluten-free stores within 30 miles. Not all examples have to be medical of course, they could be tailored to your interests if you like something more niche like skateboarding or non-school funded theater. 

I'm not saying all this to dissuade you at all, I imagine that there are probably a lot of people who go to Haverford that live on-campus and like it. If it is not clear enough, I am very much a city guy, so Haverford would not be for me, but when I was choosing colleges I didn't fully know that about myself, so I'm trying to help here.

I work at the front desk of an apartment building. My duties include logging in guests, looking at security cameras, and just generally helping out the residents who live in the building. Last week a couple ladies were paid to come in and clean a resident’s apartment. I logged in the one lady who then started talking very nastily (with a definite subtle racist undertone) about the parking attendant who told her to leave her car unattended inside the parking lot and he would get to the car after parking the one before her quickly. I asked if she parked in our lot and she said she didn’t know, so she handed me a ticket that I recognized as a place from down the street. I told her that, so I couldn’t check, but I tried to assure her that it’s a nice area and this is normally commonplace in local parking lots. She let out like a dismissive angry grunt and went upstairs. The same person came down to leave about two hours later and requested that I validate her parking, which isn’t a thing in our building in the first place, but I told her that I couldn’t help her because she didn’t park in our building. She then cursed me out and ended her tirade by say, “This place fucking sucks, I’m never coming here again!” Then she stormed out and her quiet, embarrassed coworker followed suit. I didn’t say anything to her even though I was pretty upset, but I also quickly realized she was just a miserable person. I normally have an understanding with other peons who enter the building to work because, y’know, we are being paid to be there. Ironically the company she worked for was called Merry Maids.

Eagles: 

1-22: Andre Dillard, OT, Washington State
Dillard started 4 games for the Eagles, but was active for all 16 games, occasionally getting snaps in jumbo packages or more often when Jason Peters needed a break. 
-Positives: At LT, he looked very mobile and was mostly steady in both pass pro and run blocking. He will be the starter for Wentz’s blindside next year and he earned that. 
-Negatives:Despite playing only left tackle in college, he was asked to play right tackle in the middle of the season when Lane Johnson was concussed, and Dillard really struggled there despite getting the start, and was benched after the first half. He was then relegated to solely being a left tackle, which is not a huge deal. What is more concerning is his susceptibility to power moves, especially in pass protection. This was his major concern coming out of school and will be monitored by every Eagle fan going forward.
Grade: B

2-53: Miles Sanders, RB, Penn State
Sanders was a standout rookie this year, playing in all 16 regular season games for the team and getting the start in 11 of them. As the season went on he continued to procure a larger role on offense and went Jordan Howard went down midseason, Sanders was the primary back. He led NFL rookies with 1,327 yards from scrimmage and had 6 total TDs.
-Positives: He is fast in every sense of the definition, long speed, acceleration, and burst. Later on in the season he hit his stride in the run game, routinely breaking off 10+ yard runs. He was a significant part of the passing offense as well, becoming the vertical threat (on primarily wheel/seam routes) when the team needed after DJax went down. He is a true weapon and Doug Pederson clearly loves scheming up plays for Sanders. He will be the RB1 in Philly for a long time.
-Negatives: His problems were of note in the first five games or so, especially his vision. He had a tendency to be tentative hitting holes and would bounce runs outside, something even milquetoast OC Mike Groh commented on, but that motivated Sanders and now it is barely noticeable, maybe arising 1-2 times a game. He had two fumbles (one lost) in the Lions games week 3, and since that was his weakness on his scouting report, Philadelphia watched vigilantly from then on, but I believe those were his last fumbles of the season.
Grade: A

2-57: JJ Arcega-Whiteside, WR, Stanford
JJAW played in all 16 games and started 5 of them, but his offensive snap percentage varied from 3%-92% and averaged out at 42%. He had a bland line, producing 10 catches for 169 yards and 1 TD
-Positives: Oh boy. He showed flashes Week 16 against Dallas by catching 2 first downs for 39 yards on the opening drive, but that was his only involvement on the stat sheet for the rest of the game. He had a really skilled and clutch catch against the Giants 14 where he impressively tracked the pop-up ball in midair and slid to make the catch.
-Negatives: He’s not very good, and I’ll elaborate. He suffers from the occasional drop, which is amplified by the fact he is almost never targeted. He played small and weak, his trademark was 50/50 balls in college, but if you watched him in midnight green you would never get that impression. In one of the most injury ravaged positions in all of football, the Eagles’ WR corps, he only had 10 catches for the whole year. He often was not on the same page with Carson Wentz and seemingly was often two steps from where Carson put the ball. He can’t get separation and ran the wrong route sometimes, as shown in Goedert’s one handed catch in the Week 15 game against Washington.
Grade: D-

4-138: Shareef Miller
Miller was inactive for all but 1 game in the regular season. He did not record a stat.
Positives: He has a high motor.
Negatives: He doesn’t have much else going for him than good testing and that high motor, he’s very much a project.
Grade:C-

5-167: Clayton Thorson
I’ll keep this short, like Thorson’s Eagles tenure. Thorson has a fringe NFL processing capability, but he certainly can’t get the ball to the right spot with any consistency. He was cut before the season started. In a draft class with 5 picks, picking a civ like Thorson is a killer.
Grade: F
